chapters.summary: Dr. Ayesha Delany-Brumsey identifies herself as Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety, joined by Saloni Sethi, Commissioner of the Mayor's Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, to update on the transition.
chapters.title: Commissioner Delany-Brumsey introduces OCS and NGBV leadership

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: My name is Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Farias and members of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Ayesha Delaney-Brumsey, and I'm the Commissioner of the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'm joined by Saloni Sethi, Commissioner of the Mayor's Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, or NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to speak with you today and provide an update on the ongoing transition of NGBV under OCS.

chapters.summary: Delany-Brumsey says OCS advances a coordinated, whole-of-government approach to safety, established by Executive Order 15 in March 2026, bringing gun violence, hate crimes, crisis response, victim services, and domestic and gender-based violence prevention together.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey describes OCS mission and EO 15 rationale

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Office of Community Safety advances a coordinated, whole-of-government approach to preventing violence and promoting safety across New York City.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Established by Executive Order 15 in March 2026, OCS brings together efforts to prevent gun violence and hate crimes, strengthen crisis response, support victims and survivors, and prevent domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Central to this approach is the recognition that community safety includes safety in our homes and relationships and protection from gender-based violence in all its forms.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Bringing NGBV into OCS allows us to strengthen coordination across government while continuing to build on existing expertise, programs, and partnerships.

chapters.summary: Delany-Brumsey says NGBV supports victims and survivors through collaboration with agencies, community partners, survivors, and philanthropy, and oversees prevention and intervention services including the city's five borough-based Family Justice Centers.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey outlines NGBV services and Family Justice Centers

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The NGBV team supports victims and survivors of domestic and gender-based violence and other crimes, as well as their families and communities, through collaboration with government agencies, community partners, survivors, and philanthropy.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The team works to reduce barriers, address gaps in services, and create pathways to safety through program development, legislative and policy advocacy, research, and capacity building.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV also oversees a portfolio of prevention and intervention services, including the city's five borough-based family justice centers, or FJCs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Since March, NGBV has continued to advance this mission, strengthen services, and deliver critical support to victims and survivors across New York City.

chapters.summary: Delany-Brumsey cites a $15.7 million budget increase, Home Plus expansion to $4.3 million, immigration and family law services increased 20 percent to $3.9 million, matrimonial right-to-counsel funding, and new mental health, case management, youth prevention, and community-based services.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey details FY27 budget investments for NGBV

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Mamdani administration allocated $15.7 million in new and funding to NGBV's fiscal year 27 budget, the largest such increase since the office's mission was expanded in 2018

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: to include all forms of gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This is reflective of the administration and OCS's commitment to this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This funding will support programs and services, including legal services and mental health prevention and community-based services.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: In the fiscal year 27 budget, we expanded Home Plus to $4.3 million to help survivors remain safely housed through security improvements and flexible funding, while also providing flexible funding at the Family Justice Centers to help survivors meet immediate and essential needs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Together, these programs help survivors maintain housing stability by addressing immediate safety and financial needs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have also strengthened access to legal services.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Funding for immigration and family law services at the Family Justice Centers increased by 20%, bringing the city's annual investment to $3.9 million.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also secured funding in fiscal year 27 and out for the Domestic Violence Matrimonial Right to Counsel pilot program, helping ensure that survivors

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: survivors continue to have access to critical legal representation in matrimonial proceedings.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: At the same time, this administration continues to prioritize investments that respond to needs identified by survivors, providers, advocates, and community partners.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Many of these investments also reflect years of advocacy from those working directly with survivors who have helped identify service gaps and inform the city's response.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This includes a $3.7 million annual investment in mental health services at the Family Justice Centers,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: allowing added capacity throughout the program, including services for children impacted by domestic violence,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: a 20% increase for case management, navigation, and children's services at the FJCs, and a 20% increase for youth-focused prevention through the Relationship Abuse and Prevention Program, or RAP.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also invested $3 million annually in new community-based, culturally specific services for survivors of gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We expect to share programs outlined by year's end and invite feedback from stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Crime Victims Assistance Program, or CVAP, provides critical advocacy and support to victims and survivors of domestic violence and other crimes through NYPD precincts and special victims divisions.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: While precinct-based advocates play an important role in supporting survivors, we also know that many victims of crime may never engage with law enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV's recently

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Release solicitation provides up to $15.2 million annually for the Crime Victims Assistance Program and further strengthens community-based responses for New Yorkers impacted by crime and abuse

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: by creating community-based access points so that the critical support CVAP provides can extend beyond precinct-based settings.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Through these new access points in each borough, survivors who may not feel comfortable reporting to law enforcement will be able to receive advocacy and support, including in-person accompaniment for those who may choose to report with the help of an advocate in community-based settings,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: strengthening connections between law enforcement and local providers.

chapters.summary: Delany-Brumsey says some titles and structures may change, but NGBV's mission and programs will not, and it will remain a distinct entity within OCS with dedicated leadership and direct access to OCS leadership and the Deputy Mayor.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey assures NGBV remains distinct under OCS

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: As this transition moves forward, some organizational structures and leadership titles may change, but NGBV's mission and the critical programs and services it oversees will not.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV will remain a distinct entity within OCS with dedicated leadership, a clear mandate, and a strong programmatic identity.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The expertise of the NGBV team, as well as all the teams that have been incorporated into OCS, will continue to inform decision-making, with direct and regular access to myself as the Commissioner, OCS leadership, and the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Bringing NGBV into OCS also creates opportunities for stronger coordination across the city's community safety work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Domestic and gender-based violence intersects with many of the challenges OCS is charged with addressing, including gun violence, mental health, crisis response, and support for victims and survivors of crime and violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: His research on the relation between domestic violence and shooting incidents in New York City found that communities with high rates of gun violence also experience high rates of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that access to firearms can increase the risk of serious injury or death in abusive relationships, and firearms also can be used to threaten, intimidate, and control survivors.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Moreover, young people exposed to violence in the home are more likely to both experience and perpetrate violence, including gun violence, as they grow up.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Children exposed to domestic violence are almost three times more likely to experience domestic violence as adults, and childhood exposure to family violence is also a strong predictor of domestic violence perpetration later in life.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Bringing this work together creates opportunities to strengthen prevention and intervention efforts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Further, survivors with mental health needs may face unique barriers to accessing both the domestic violence and mental health systems, particularly when navigating multiple systems that may not fully address their needs.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: At the same time, domestic and gender-based violence can have significant and lasting impact on survivors'mental health.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Further connecting NGB's expertise with mental health and crisis response can help align services, provide more responsive and trauma-informed care, and address survivors'needs more holistically.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: These connections reflect our vision for OCS.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: A public health approach to safety that recognizes both the immediate and long-term impacts of violence, coordination across prevention, intervention, victim and survivor services, and crisis response will help us make a

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: use of the city's expertise and resources while helping keep domestic and gender-based violence central to our community safety work.

chapters.summary: Delany-Brumsey says the Deputy Mayor will participate in NGBV advisory councils quarterly and that OCS supports Intro 1079 on hotline reporting with adjustments because the NYC Hope Hotline also supports survivors of other crimes.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey discusses advisory engagement and supports Intro 1079

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Another important part of this work is maintaining direct communication with survivors, advocates, service providers, OCS, NGBV, and City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Deputy Mayor Francois will participate in NGBV advisory councils quarterly, meeting alongside OCS and NGBV leadership, providing a regular opportunity to hear directly from stakeholders, assess progress, and discuss needs and priorities.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Staff, providers, advocates, and other stakeholders will continue to be engaged throughout the transition and implementation process.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We appreciate the opportunity to provide positions on the legislation under consideration today.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We support Bill 1079 to 2026 reporting on hotline survivors for gender-based violence, with some adjustments to reflect that the New York City Hope Hotline supports survivors of gender-based violence and other crimes.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We would be happy to discuss those adjustments with the council following the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We look forward to continued collaboration with the council, our sister agencies, survivors, advocates, service providers, and community-based partners as we move this work forward.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Together, we will continue to strengthen services, address gaps, improve coordination across systems, and ensure that victims and survivors have access to the support they need.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today, and we welcome any questions.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: questions you may have.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Thank you so much for testifying.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined by Speaker Julie Menon.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll kick it over to you for questions first.

chapters.summary: Speaker Julie Menin asks what specific additional resources NGBV will access under OCS. Delany-Brumsey cites the $15.7 million budget increase and a coordinated public-health approach to safety.
chapters.title: Speaker Menin questions OCS on specific new resources for NGBV

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Farias.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I want to thank you for holding this very, very important hearing and for all of the advocates and groups who are here today.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I know this is a very difficult topic, and so we really appreciate you being here.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So, I mean, I think my first question really has to do with the Office of Community Safety

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: having communicated that one reason for moving the mayor's office to end domestic and gender-based violence, or of course, NGBV, under OCS is that NGBV would have access to more resources,

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: be part of a coordinated citywide community safety strategy.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: What specific additional resources will NGBV have access to under OCS that they didn't have before?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: One of the resources that I can point to, and thank you for that question, is that in this current fiscal year, we increased the budget for NGBV by $15.7 million, which is the largest increase that NGBV has received since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's one significant type of resource that NGBV will have access to.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: In addition, the creation of OCS more generally is a part of the administration's focus on ensuring that we are providing a comprehensive approach.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: to public safety so that the people in places at the most risk for harm, the types of violence that are most intractable, have access to a coordinated approach.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know, as I testified, that people who experience domestic and gender-based violence often live in neighborhoods with higher rates of gun violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also understand the significant mental health and substance use relationship between the impacts of domestic violence on behavioral health needs and the relationship between mental health and substance use.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So combining OCS, combining NGBV into OCS allows NGBV and the other offices within OCS to work in a more coordinated way to build out a strategy that supports

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: all survivors even more effectively.

chapters.summary: Menin says NGBV previously had a freestanding office and dedicated commissioner, asking whether the new structure sends a wrong signal to survivors and advocates. Delany-Brumsey says OCS elevates the work, while Sethi says leadership and staff remain in place.
chapters.title: Menin challenges loss of freestanding commissioner

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: But don't you agree that you had a freestanding office with a commissioner that was dedicated to this important topic?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: You now no longer have a commissioner, and you've now put it under a new entity.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Don't you think that sends a wrong signal to survivors and to all the groups on the ground who are doing this important work?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The signal that I hope it sends is that this is a effort, or this is a focus of the administration that is extremely important.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCS is a high priority for this administration.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The work within it is

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The incorporation of NGBV within that work is part of the administration's effort to not diminish, but to elevate and escalate the work of that office.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I can jump in and say, you know, I think even with this transition, the role of NGBV very much remains the same, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think for me, for the leadership team, for the staff, most of us are all still here.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: The entire leadership team is still here, and we're still here because what we know is our role is to make sure that as we work with OCS and work with our partners, we're continuing to elevate issues that are meaningful and important to survivors and to our providers.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And we think that that's so far, you know, we've been doing a pretty good job of that, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And that reflects in the funding and in our ongoing work.

chapters.summary: Menin asks how many staff work at OCS and NGBV. Delany-Brumsey says OCS has about 100 staff total, while Sethi says NGBV has 79 staff lines with 59 filled, about a 25 percent vacancy rate.
chapters.title: Menin asks OCS and NGBV staffing numbers and vacancies

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And how many staff are currently hired by OCS or currently working right now at OCS?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: OCS is approximately 100 staff total across all of our offices.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That includes...

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So we have 79 staff lines, and currently 59 of those positions are filled.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Wait, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: NGBV has 79 staff lines, and currently we have 59 of those positions filled.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So it's about a 25% vacancy rate.

chapters.summary: Menin asks what is being done to fill vacancies. Sethi says historical city hiring freezes caused the backlog, now lifted, and NGBV is working with OCS and the Deputy Mayor to fill positions, recently filling a Staten Island Family Justice Center director role vacant for three years.
chapters.title: Menin asks efforts to fill NGBV vacancies

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And what are the efforts to fill those vacancies?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So we've actually been doing really...

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: The vacancy rates are from historical hiring freezes that the city's been under for many, many years.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so now that those are lifted, we've actually been working with Commissioner Aisha and the Deputy Mayor of Community Safety's team to move these vacancies forward as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: One thing I want to highlight is, you know, one of the positions we filled recently was at our Staten Island FJC for the Director of Community Programs and Partnerships.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And that role had been sort of vacant for three years, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: But that's the reality in which we were living in terms of city hiring and freezes and processes.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so we're doing our best to kind of move through that backlog with support from DMCS and OCS.

chapters.summary: Menin says gender-based violence groups and survivors fear the administration is minimizing the work. Delany-Brumsey and Sethi deny minimizing, citing ongoing meetings, site visits, and continued access to NGBV leadership.
chapters.title: Menin relays provider concerns that restructuring minimizes GBV work

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: We have heard from many of the gender-based violence groups as well as survivors concerns that the administration is minimizing the gender-based violence work by this move.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: And so what would you say to those concerns?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Definitely want to ensure that our partners, advocates, providers, survivors, that we are not minimizing the importance of this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: As you heard from Commissioner Sethi, the incorporation of NGBV into OCS is an effort to escalate and elevate this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are working very closely across the entire OCS team and with NGBV to ensure that we continue to engage very closely with our partners.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I have attended the NGBV Advisory Council that Deputy Mayor has.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We will continue to do that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We've held dozens of conversations with providers, advocates, survivors.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have conducted site visits.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are going to continue to work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: very closely with our partners to ensure that the work of NGBV, the focus that has been built over the past 25 years, remains not only intact, but is strengthened as we build together.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: No, I mean, I think, yeah, I think all of that, you know, makes sense.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think, again, what I would invite all of our survivors community or advocate community or provider community is to keep reaching out and keep, you know, connecting with us because we're here.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: You know, I'm like, I want to say, I'm still here.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: My email hasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: My number hasn't changed.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So please reach out and we will do our best to make sure that we're continuing to connect.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And because I truly believe like this work is going to be stronger if we move forward together.

chapters.summary: Menin says she believes NGBV should be freestanding with a commissioner, expresses disagreement with the restructuring, and turns questioning back to Chair Farías.
chapters.title: Menin ends questions and disagrees with removing commissioner

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: Okay, that's the end of my questions.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I just do want to say, I frankly do believe there should be a commissioner of this entity, and I think it should be freestanding.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: I think that is really important.

utterances.speaker: Julie Menin
utterances.text: So I just want to express my disagreement with that, but I'm going to turn it over to the chair.

chapters.summary: Farías notes more than 249,000 domestic violence incident reports in 2024 and asks where OCS places gender-based violence. Delany-Brumsey says it is a top priority and that safety cannot be improved without addressing domestic and gender-based violence.
chapters.title: Chair Farías asks where OCS places GBV among priorities

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Speaker, for joining us and for the questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I have similar sentiments about, you know, looking at the way we're merging in some of our other commissioners.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I actually have a specific question to that as well.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But just primarily, I'd like to start.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Gender-based violence remains a significant issue in New York City with 249,000.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Over 249,000 domestic violence incident reports in 2024 alone.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Where does the Office of Community Safety see gender-based violence in terms of priorities to be addressed?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: in this administration?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Gender-based violence is a top priority for this administration and for the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that we cannot improve safety without addressing the impact of domestic and gender-based violence across New York.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I, as a commissioner, am working very closely with Commissioner Sethi to ensure that as we are developing the ongoing strategy for the office, that domestic and gender-based violence remains a significant priority

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: and that it not only is a focus of our work, but we are building it in such a way that it will continue to be strengthened, that the

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: office itself can benefit from the other offices, that the office can also lend its expertise to the other offices that are part of it, so that in the years to come, New Yorkers who are experiencing gender-based violence, who may also be experiencing hate crimes, who may also have a mental health need,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: that they are going to, one, they have access to a much more comprehensive and holistic approach to this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And it's a recognition that the work that NGBV has done over the past 25 years is strong, needs to continue to be strong, and needs to continue to be elevated.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I can only point to the early signs of the administration's commitment to this work, the $15.7 million that had been invested, the continued and ongoing connection between, or building connection between myself, the deputy mayor,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: and the supporters and advocates and providers to say how much this is a continued priority.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether six executive director titles and four deputy commissioner titles at NGBV will change. Delany-Brumsey says OCS is reviewing titles across the combined offices and has not made decisions, aiming to reflect seniority and expertise.
chapters.title: Farías questions title changes for executive directors and deputies

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then just to...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Similarly to what the speaker was asking about commissioners at these title change will go to executive director once the office officially moves to the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: According to some reports, there are approximately six executive director titles across NGBV that are now reporting to the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Will the existing executive director titles change as a result of the commissioner becoming an executive director?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then additionally, there are four deputy commissioners within NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are those titles also going to change?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The combination of the offices under OCS means that there's lots of different titles because each office had its own title structure.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so the title differences do not just impact NGBV, they impact the entire Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're engaged in a process right now to look across our team to see what makes sense in terms of making sure we have titles that reflect the seniority, the expertise, and that allow people to do the work they continue to do.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have not made any decisions because we are making sure that we are doing this carefully and assessing how titles.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Will continue to broadcast the seniority, expertise, and influence that are both the leadership and the rest of the team has.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether NGBV employees will keep equivalent salaries next year. Delany-Brumsey says combining four offices with different pay scales requires careful equitable review, no significant decisions have been made, and the goal is appropriate staffing.
chapters.title: Farías asks about salary equity for NGBV appointees

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So we'll just stay in communication on how that continues to move forward.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: While there's restructuring and changing of title,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: the amount of work conducted by NGBV will remain the same or increase.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do you expect all appointees and employees at NGBV to keep a salary next year that is equivalent to this year?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So again, we are looking, as you can imagine, combining four offices means there's also different pay scales.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: There's a lot of work to be done to ensuring that we are being equitable.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have not made any significant decisions at this moment because we are trying to work very closely with the office as well as our city partners to ensure that any changes that we make are equitable.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, the goal is to ensure that we have appropriate staffing to do this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: As the work continues and builds, we will need additional staff, we will need additional funding, and that is the work of myself, the leadership team that I work with, the administration to ensure that the work is appropriately staffed.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: As you heard from Commissioner Sethi, we have actually been able to fill some vacancies that have not been filled in the past, and so we are working towards ensuring that we have the robust staffing that we need to do the growing and important work.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how regularly the Deputy Mayor for Community Safety meets with the Mayor and NGBV on gender-based violence. Delany-Brumsey says the Deputy Mayor meets regularly with the Mayor on OCS, and meets weekly or more with her and Commissioner Sethi.
chapters.title: Farías asks frequency of Deputy Mayor and Mayor meetings on NGBV

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How regularly will the Deputy Mayor for Community Safety be meeting with the Mayor?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: about NGBV and gender-based violence issues in New York City, and how often do we anticipate the assistant deputy meeting with NGBV about gender-based violence?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Do we have a structure there, a strategy?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So the deputy mayor meets regularly with the mayor around OCS, including focusing on NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The deputy mayor and myself meet regularly, weekly, sometimes significantly more than weekly.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Myself and commissioner meet absolutely more than weekly.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have ongoing communication and coordination with the deputy mayor's team that includes project meetings, that includes strategic planning meetings, and that includes brief updates.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we have a significant amount of coordination that's happening at all levels across the office.

chapters.summary: Farías notes the NGBV Advisory Council sent a February meeting request and recommendations that went unanswered before Executive Order 15. Delany-Brumsey acknowledges early slowness and says the administration later responded and met with the council, while Sethi says new funding reflected advisory asks.
chapters.title: Farías asks how OCS will engage NGBV Advisory Council recommendations

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In February, the NGBV Advisory Council sent a meeting request to the administration and a list of community-informed recommendations, but did not receive a response before the announcement of Executive Order 15.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How will OCS engage with recommendations from NGBV's Advisory Council in the future?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we acknowledged some slowness, some missteps in some of the early communication.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: However, the administration has been working very hard to correct that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We did respond to that letter.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We also met direct myself, the deputy mayor of community safety, met with the NGBV advisory council.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are continuing to have those meetings.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are continuing to have site visits.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And in that letter,

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We responded with how some of the feedback from the advocates and advisory council had influenced some of the work that NGBV did, including some of the recent investments.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I can turn to Commissioner Sate for some additional details there.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think, you know, when you look at the new funding that we received, some of those asks really came directly from the advisory council letter and in an effort to be responsive to what our advocates were asking for, including the funding for culturally specific services, including the funding for,

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: you know, grassroots and survivor-led orgs, and including funding for existing programs, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: I think what we came up with in that $15.7 million was reflective of new things, as well as understanding that our existing programs also need more because they're doing a lot with very little and have been.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so we need to end what we're continuing to see people with higher levels of need.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I'd say in addition to sort of ongoing partnership with the advisory council, we're also working on site visits and listening sessions that we will continue to do and hosted one just yesterday at the Bronx FJC with a deputy mayor and her team, which was really, really nice.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Great, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Also, apologies.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We've been joined by Councilmember Jennifer Gutierrez as well.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether moving NGBV to OCS could slow open-data reporting. Delany-Brumsey says systems and processes are being put in place to meet obligations, and Sethi says the data and IGA teams remain the same.
chapters.title: Farías asks if OCS move will slow open-data reporting

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just want to talk a little bit about data and reporting.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: NGBV is in compliance with the open data law and regularly uploads reports to open data on time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Will the move to OCS potentially slow that processing time down?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How will OCS ensure that it does not?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of our offices have a variety of reports that they are required to submit.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: As part of our efforts to consolidate the office, we are ensuring that we have the systems and processes in place so that we do not slow that down, that we are continuing to meet our obligations, and we have continued to do that to date.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah, and I'd say for right now, like our data team is the same.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Our, you know, IGA team, small IGA team is the same.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so we're kind of working through those same channels to provide reports as requested as usual.

chapters.summary: Farías cites the annual fact sheet, Family Justice Center client satisfaction surveys, and Fatality Review Committee reports. Delany-Brumsey says the approval process remains largely the same, and Sethi says both commissioners now review reports but it has not been a problem.
chapters.title: Farías asks about report approval process under new structure

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then in terms of the several key reports, as you even mentioned, around gender-based violence, including the annual fact sheet, Family Justice Center client satisfaction surveys, the Fatality Review Committee reports, among many others,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: what's the approval process for publishing these reports under the new structure?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Will there be any changes?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The approval process will remain largely the same.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have an expert team that understands this work and understands how to create and draft highly.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Accurate and effective reports.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we will continue with the approval process, you know, largely the same.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: I think, yeah, the only changes both of us will be reviewing, but so far that's been totally not a problem.

chapters.summary: Farías notes NGBV manages $13 million in Council discretionary funding and asks how many contracts it holds. Sethi says NGBV manages 90 contracts, and Delany-Brumsey says HRA will continue supporting contracting while OCS builds internal capacity.
chapters.title: Farías asks how many contracts NGBV manages

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, thanks, folks.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd like to talk a little bit about contracting.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The council has frequently heard that mayoral agencies can struggle to manage procurement processes because they lack the staffing infrastructure to manage contracts.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: NGBV currently manages $13 million of council discretionary funding and has support from HRA staff to do so.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How many contracts is NGBV currently managing?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In the portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Do you want to say the total number of contracts?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We have a total of 90 contracts currently.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Nine zero?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Nine zero.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It was like 90.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: It's a big portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I would just add to that, just for context, that HRA will continue to support NGBV's contracting as OCS builds out our own internal contracting function.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're building out a contracting function not just to support NGBV, but to support the entire office, which has even more than the 90 contracts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we're doing that work in partnership with HRA, as well as the other agencies that currently support our contracting work, in combination with other mayoral offices and city agencies that support contracting so that we can ensure we're building out a contracting shop that has the staffing

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: and the capacity and the structure in place to do this work well.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that contracting...

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: well is both about meeting city obligations, but it's also about ensuring that the providers that we work with, our contractors, are able to do the good work that we are paying them for.

chapters.summary: Farías asks about the purpose of the new CVAP RFP. Delany-Brumsey says CVAP embeds advocates in every precinct and adds community access points for victims who do not report to police, while Sethi says it increases access and diversifies providers.
chapters.title: Farías asks goal of new Crime Victims Assistance Program RFP

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That's great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: You answered my next question, so I'm contracting.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What's the goal of the new RFP regarding the Crime Victims Assistance Program?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I'll turn this to Commissioner Sethi for the details, but one thing that I will say is that we're really excited to have the Crime Victims Assistance Program, RFP, out.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We really encourage people to apply.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The Crime Victims Assistance Program ensures that we are embedding victims'advocates in every single...

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Precinct across New York City and it is also focused on ensuring that we have crime victims advocates and community-based partners so that we can ensure that for victims who are not comfortable reporting to the police that they have a place where they can receive victim services.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We know that it is essential that there is universal active access to victim services

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: within NYPD precincts.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a core tenant of this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We intend to continue that going forward because we want to make sure that we are meeting victims wherever they are.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're really excited to be able to expand that work so that we have additional access points in the community because unfortunately we know that so often victims don't report.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And those victims advocates will be there whether or not someone does report.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: If they are interested in reporting, they will accompany that person to the police precinct to help them report if they wish.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah, no, I agree.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think, you know, for me and for Angie,

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: I think our goals in this work and all of the work we do are really, really quite consistent and similar, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So one thing is always about increasing access, reducing barriers, increasing access to resources for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think this does that by, you know, keeping the precinct-based services, but also adding community-based, you know, touch points for these services, for advocacy, for potentially support for survivors that may be

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: afraid to walk into a precinct to do that with accompaniment, with a peer navigator.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: That's a huge shift, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think, but an important one that is about increasing access for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And then the other thing, you know, I know that our office thinks about all the time is, you know, survivors'experiences are diverse.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: There's a million different experiences of survivorship, and our provider community reflects that diversity and should continue to reflect that diversity, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We should have different providers for different survivors with different needs.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so one of the other things, and not just in CVAP, but with our FJCs, with the contracting we've done over the years, is adding borough-based options allows us to diversify providers as well, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And we kind of have different providers doing the same work, which, again, is about, you know, making it easier for survivors to access what they need, where they need, and with an organization they feel most comfortable with.

chapters.summary: Farías appreciates the borough-based RFP response, reserves the rest of her time, and turns questioning over to Council Member Aldebol, followed by Council Members Gutiérrez and Santosuosso.
chapters.title: Farías thanks agency panel and turns to Council Member Aldebol

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for the response.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I feel I would agree that most of us kind of appreciate a borough-based response when it comes to an RFP.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We don't always get that opportunity to have RFPs that can cover the multitude of the city and making sure everyone has a provider that's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm going to reserve the rest of my time to get to some council member questions, and I'll turn it over to Council Member Aldebar, followed by...

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Gutiérrez, then Sanzuzuoso.

chapters.summary: Aldebol follows up on NGBV's 79 staff lines and 59 filled positions, asking how much vacancy is due to turnover. Sethi says turnover has been low and many staff have been with NGBV for 10 or more years because of the mission.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks about NGBV vacancy turnover

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: I have a couple of follow-up questions.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Both Speaker Menon and Councilmember Fadies asked about restructuring and staffing.

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: You said that there were 79 lines currently, 59 filled, attributed

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: you know, the vacancy rate to a backlog of hiring, how much of that is attributed to turnover?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So honestly, our office has, you know, it's had some turnover, but not very much.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We've had, what I'm always, what I'm always personally really surprised by is how many folks in our office have been with NGBV for 10 plus years, including some folks that have been with NGBV before it was NGBV or even in office.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So I think it really does speak to kind of the, you know, people coming to this because it's passion work and to the sort of the meaning that they find in the work.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether staffing reductions are expected as roles change. Sethi says it is too soon to know the structure, and Delany-Brumsey says the charge is to build a comprehensive approach and appropriately staff and expand domestic violence work.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks if restructuring will reduce NGBV staffing

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you foresee reductions in staffing as roles are changed and the office gets put under?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah, it's too soon to be able to say what our literal structure will look like.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: However, what I can say is that we know that the charge we've been given is to build a more comprehensive

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: approach to community safety and that includes ensuring that we are appropriately staffing the work around domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So our work is to really expand and to ensure that we're building out our staffing.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So while I

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: It's too soon to know exactly how far we will be able to expand.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is the charge that's put forward.

chapters.summary: Aldebol asks whether the move to OCS will dramatically restructure staff roles. Delany-Brumsey says no dramatic change is anticipated for NGBV programs, but OCS will restructure to provide expertise and operational support; Sethi says core functions remain prevention, direct services, advocacy, research, evaluation, and training.
chapters.title: Aldebol asks if staff roles will change dramatically under OCS

utterances.speaker: Shirley Aldebol
utterances.text: Do you foresee a restructuring or dramatic change in staff roles given the move to OCS?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I don't see a dramatic change in the way that NGBV is staffing their programs at this point.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We have not been able to.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I anticipate that what we will be doing is ensuring that we have the appropriate staffing across our entire team.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that as we're building out our survivor and victim services, we will continue to do that work with NGBV, with the other offices.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: But we will be restructuring, but it's too soon to know exactly what that will look like.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The purpose of the restructuring will be to ensure that we have all of the necessary expertise to do the work of domestic and gender-based violence prevention, all of the necessary expertise to do the work of hate crime prevention.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Of building out behavioral health services, of preventing gun and community-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So that's the North Star for that kind of restructuring, and that all of those offices have the kind of operational support that they need to do their work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: whether that's contracting, budgets, administrative support, all of that, which is really necessary as you grow an office from what it is today to what we will hopefully be in the future, which is significantly larger.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I'll say all the core functions of NGBV, I think, are critical to what OCS is going to do, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Which the core functions are prevention, direct services, advocacy, research, evaluation, and training.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Those are things that are always going to be part of whatever we're doing as NGBV and as part of OCS.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to Councilmember Gutierrez.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether the move under OCS could create delays for people calling 311 or searching for NGBV. Delany-Brumsey says no extra layer is anticipated, NGBV's website will remain, and OCS will link to it.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether 311 access will be affected by restructuring

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you all so much.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I had also just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: One logistically under the Mayor's Office and gender-based violence under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Does that affect...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: The way that anyone would maybe call 311 for more information related to this office.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there another person or another, like, is there a delay?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Because it's now not its own standalone office.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: It's under this, like, bigger and larger umbrella.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: So just logistically.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, no, no, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: They're an anticipated extra person, extra 10 seconds of, like, research.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And if you don't know, let's figure it out.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I was just thinking about how to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think it's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I don't anticipate that there will be an extra layer of access.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: For example, we will continue to have the NGB.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV's website, as we build out our OCS website, people will still be able to find that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The OCS website will link to the NGBV website.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Our goal will be to ensure as we're building this out that people have very easy, very quick access to community safety work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is a North Star for all of the work that we're doing.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so I would want to ensure that as we're building this, we will continue to work very closely with the leadership across.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: NGBV across our other offices to say how are New Yorkers finding out about our work and how do we ensure that even more New Yorkers find out about our work that we are easier and easier to find no matter what.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Well, I would love to circle back at some point to see if that is the case.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think that sometimes, and again, this is someone that's like calling 311.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I think if it's online, it's a little different.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: But just speaking with some of the folks at the call center, sometimes they're not necessarily privy to some of the changes that are happening, either that we legislate or even that City Hall does.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: And so it would just be helpful or maybe just to connect with them and ensuring that like they're up to date.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Again, don't want to delay an emergency.

chapters.summary: After Gutiérrez asks OCS to update 311 call center staff, Delany-Brumsey agrees to circle back and asks the Council to report any delays so OCS can address them.
chapters.title: Delany-Brumsey welcomes feedback on access issues

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: No, I think that's great.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And one thing that we would love to be able to circle back on that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And if you are hearing about ways in which people are not finding out about us or can't, you know, there is a delay, please let us know because we'd love to try to address that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Whenever we do hear about a concern, we want to make sure we work to address it.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So if you are hearing things, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We'd love to.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I haven't heard, but I just want to make.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez cites high domestic violence rates in her district and asks how NGBV will partner with OCS divisions on public housing. Delany-Brumsey says NGBV staff joined Deputy Mayor-led public housing safety meetings with the Office of Neighborhood Safety and that joint work is being strengthened.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks about public housing partnerships and resources

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: sure we're ahead of it because I think it's it's difficult to kind of like restructure this um and then my last question that I am just curious um pre-pandemic um

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: a night to develop it in my district books where houses had some of the higher rates of domestic violence incidents um and so

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: I'm familiar with some of the folks on the ground under the various divisions of Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Is there anything specific that your office is being asked to do in partnership with some of these divisions in public housing specifically?

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Like, is this merger going to allow us to...

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Have more resources just to do more and specifically in public housing?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Yeah, that's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: The deputy mayor actually recently ran a set of meetings to address some key safety issues in locations across the city, public housing locations, other locations.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And one of the things that we noticed early on is that we needed to have someone within those meetings who had domestic and gender-based violence expertise.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we included one of the staff members from NGBV in those meetings, in addition to staff members from the Office of Neighborhood Safety, who do a lot of our work in NITRA developments.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so that's just one example of how we're trying to get these teams to work even more closely together so that we can say, for our team that's supporting NITRA developments around reducing violence, we know that so often some of that violence has a root in domestic

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so how do we ensure that we are both bringing resources as well as expertise?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And one of the things that I noticed when I first came on as commissioner is some of that work was already happening.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: These offices, while separate, were doing some work together.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: They have some joint providers.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so we're really just building on that foundation and trying to make it stronger and stronger.

chapters.summary: Gutiérrez asks whether NGBV receives additional resources under OCS. Delany-Brumsey says NGBV received $15.7 million in additional funding this year, the largest increase since 2018.
chapters.title: Gutiérrez asks whether OCS brings additional dollars for NGBV

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: There's no additional dollars or resources under this new Office of Community Safety for your office?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: For NGBV?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We absolutely did have additional funding.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We had $15.7 million in additional funding just this year, which is the largest increase that we have seen for NGBV since 2018.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Okay, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Jennifer Gutiérrez
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I'll turn it over to Council Member Santos-Wilson.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso honors constituent Maria Inez Granda, killed in an extreme act of domestic violence, then asks how the $15.7 million flows to CBOs and Family Justice Centers versus administrative costs. The answer says all $15.7 million is for contracted programs.
chapters.title: Santosuosso honors domestic violence victim and asks about funding flow

utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair, and thank you so much for being here.

utterances.text: I want to start by just acknowledging that we recently lost a constituent in our district to murder in an extreme act of domestic violence, Maria Inez Granda.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And so in her honor, I just want to thank all the advocates that are doing this work and thank you to the Office of Gender-Based Violence for what you do.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: With that, I have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Just to follow up on Councilmember Gutierrez's question, I think sort of what I was hearing is with that $15 million,

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: plus in additional resources.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I know in your testimony you said it looks like it will support programs and services, legal services, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I guess I'm curious how much of that will actually flow to CBOs and the providers in the family justice centers versus sort of like administrative and centralized costs.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I was like, of that $15.7 million, all of it is for programs that are contracted programs.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: So, love to hear that.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks whether current NGBV-funded contractors or providers will see any funding decrease due to the merger. The answer says no funding is being decreased, only increased.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks if providers will see funding decreases from merger

utterances.text: And I believe you said this in your testimony, and I believe it was asked out in questions, but I just want to flush it out entirely.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: For CBOs and for providers who are concerned that maybe this merger would lead to a decrease in their funding, if a contractor or a provider is currently funded by NGBV, will they see any decrease in their funding as a result of this merger directly?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: We are not currently decreasing any funding.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: We are only in the space of increasing funding.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Again, love to hear it.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Just wanted to flush it out for folks.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks if CBOs and providers will have the same access to NGBV staff amid confusion about the merger. Delany-Brumsey says staff from frontline to leadership continue working with partners and are an additional point of access.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: that would lead to a lack of access to the NGBV staff and the support that they've provided in the past.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Can you confirm that they will have just as easy of a right of access to the office as they've had in the past?

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: All of our staff from the front line to leadership continues to

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: work directly with their partners.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I would encourage everyone to continue to reach out to the people that they have been working with.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: They are also welcome to reach out to myself should they like.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're just an additional point of access.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We work extremely closely with each other.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We sit 20

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: two feet from each other.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're operating and continuing to build to a real office.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so absolutely, we want to be sure everyone that they will have the access.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And to the earlier point, if there are any issues with access that are being raised, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We'd love to address.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks how the CVAP RFP will ensure precinct-based advocates work collaboratively with NYPD rather than as siloed outside workers. Sethi says NGBV has built relationships with NYPD and cites a recent success getting posters about CVAP advocates placed in precincts.
chapters.title: Santosuosso asks how CVAP RFP ensures NYPD collaboration
