utterances.text: And then, sorry, one more thing.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: With regard to the Crime Victims Assistance Program, RFP, what work is going to be done to see that the folks who are placed in those precincts are sort of

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: working with the NYPD and the precincts in a way that is productive and collaborative and actually integrative versus as sort of an outside siloed worker.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah, that is definitely, you know, part of what NGBV has been doing since we sort of started, you know, administering CVAP as a contract.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so we will continue to do that in terms of like bridging the, you know, at PD, making sure we have the right relationships with folks that are senior enough to move a thing.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: You know, we have really close relationships with the folks that do the domestic and gender-based violence work.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And we're working on getting, you know, the CVAP advocates the support they need at the precinct level as well.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So we're here and we really hope to continue playing an active role in making sure that that relationship is working the way we think it should.

chapters.summary: Santosuosso asks whether that NYPD collaboration will change due to restructuring. Sethi says it will not and offers the poster example as a small but meaningful win.
chapters.title: Santosuosso confirms CVAP integration won't change with restructuring

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: And that won't change as a result of the MRAP.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: It won't.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: I'll just give you a really small example of a win recently.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We got PD to put up posters that had information about CVEP advocates in the precinct.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So the program had been operating for 10 years without posters saying, here's somebody you can talk to.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So I think that is a success that we were able to help coordinate with the contracted provider, with NYPD and with NGBB staff to really make that happen.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so I think that's, you know, it's small things like that that sometimes make the difference.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: I appreciate your time.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Kayla Santosuosso
utterances.text: Thanks, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

chapters.summary: Farías asks about the future of Family Justice Centers currently operated by Safe Horizon. Sethi clarifies NGBV operates the FJCs and Safe Horizon is one of 10 contracted providers, says services remain unchanged, and notes 63,000 visits annually.
chapters.title: Farías asks about future of Family Justice Centers and Safe Horizon

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm just going to jump in on a few more questions before we get to public testimony.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: In terms of contracting, what is the future of the family justice centers currently operated by Safe Horizons?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So the FJCs, which are operated by NGBV, actually SafeRise is a contracted provider at Manhattan for a few services.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We have 10 different contracted providers.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: So far, you know, we're still no change in that service.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: I think our only hope is to continue expanding because, again, what we continue to see is we are seeing, you know, tens of thousands of visits a year, you know, 63,000 visits annually.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And what we are seeing is that the people that we're serving have higher levels of need.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And so I think when I think about my role and NGBV's role, it's like how do we make sure that our providers doing this work are better resourced to do this work, which is getting more and more challenging due to the circumstances that we find ourselves in, federally especially.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how OCS will protect small community-based organizations serving specific languages or cultural communities from funding lapses during the transition. Delany-Brumsey says preventing payment gaps is a core concern, especially for small providers that cannot float expenses.
chapters.title: Farías asks how OCS will prevent funding lapses for small CBOs

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And how will the OCS ensure that small community-based organizations that are often the only program

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: providers able to offer services in specific languages or particular cultural communities not experience a lapse in any of their funding during the transition?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This is a core concern of the transition that we're working to address.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We want to make sure that when we do ultimately move contracts over, that we have the structures in place already and that that structure has been in place for weeks, months, building up so that we can transition without any gaps in payment.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We want to ensure that all of our providers, but we know it's especially crucial for our smaller providers who can't float while there's a payment gap, that we are doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's crucial for NGBV's work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's crucial for the work of the Office of Neighborhood Safety, which works with very small providers, Office of Prevention of Hate Crimes.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: All of our office really does attempt to work with both small, culturally specific organizations that are deeply embedded in their community, as well as some of our larger service providers who can cover more ground.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So we are very, very focused on ensuring that that does not.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Become an issue.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether the internal contracting database is part of the plan. Delany-Brumsey says yes, it is part of building OCS's contracting function, and Sethi says a working group with other city agencies will coordinate and communicate with providers.
chapters.title: Farías asks about internal contract database for smoother transition

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And is that also connected to the work that you're doing to having an internal contracted database where we're hoping payments and that structure continue on for a smoother transition?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's part of the work of building out our own contracting function internal to OCS.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We're aiming to do that in such a way that we can have as effective a contracting shop as possible.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I'd say that this is another thing that we're sort of doing, you know, with other city agencies that are involved.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: in this process, right, as we think about what this will take in launching, you know, a coordinated working group to really figure out what the steps are.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think, you know, for providers that are our providers, we will do our best to be in communication with you.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Please reach out and ask questions, right, because I think that's also the other piece is as this happens, how are we communicating the steps over and over again?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And I will just add to that that Commissioner Sethi is the person on the team who is managing the working group to support this build out with other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: So that focus on domestic and gender-based violence is front and center there.

chapters.summary: Farías seeks the total NGBV budget. Sethi says FY27 total is $89.1 million, with roughly $7 to $8 million for staff and the rest contracted programming and discretionary Council contracts; Delany-Brumsey confirms the $15.7 million increase is part of that total.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how OCS will facilitate relationships between domestic and gender-based violence organizations and gun violence prevention and violence interrupter programs. Delany-Brumsey cites advisory councils, cross-team work, and potential Family Justice Center-like models.
chapters.title: Farías asks how OCS will connect DV organizations with violence interrupters

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And then just a couple of few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How will OCS facilitate relationships between domestic and gender-based violence organizations and other key partners, including violence interrupter programs and gun violence prevention organizations?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's something that we are doing now and that we intend to continue to build out a variety of ways of doing that work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think it will happen in a number of ways.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Part of it is as the team grows into a more cohesive team across the office and they are sharing.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: sharing best practices, sharing ways of working, that they will naturally also be bringing their partners with them.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: Other ways that we are doing that is we, of course, have existing advisory councils.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I anticipate that as we continue to expand, we'll have existing ways to bring together our providers in other advisory bodies, meetings, and we'll work to include a range of different providers.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: We are also, as we build out new initiatives around public safety, one of the focuses of that work is to think about

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: What are initiatives that address multiple different forms of violence?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so how do we do that in a comprehensive way?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: One of the lovely things about the Family Justice Center is it's a comprehensive approach to addressing domestic and gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: It has lots of different providers embedded within it.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I could imagine models like that happening in different spaces across our work, including providers in the domestic and gender-based violence space, the gun violence space, the hate crimes prevention space.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This is...

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This is not me saying a new program.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: This is just me saying how I imagine that as we build out, we will continue to ensure that we're pulling on the right people to provide a more holistic approach to this really challenging issue.

chapters.summary: Sethi says OCS does not need everyone to be an expert in everything, but cross-training helps teams understand distinct roles and refer survivors appropriately, similar to how legal and mental health staff collaborate in Family Justice Centers.
chapters.title: Sethi explains cross-training model for DV and community violence providers

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: No, and I'll say, I think, you know, one of the things we talk about all the time, right, is like, is like,

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: One of the beautiful things about even bringing the teams together and the orgs together and doing kind of like cross-training work is really understanding what people do that's different in a way that you don't always, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And I think even as Commissioner Delaney Brumsey and I talk, like one of the things we want to avoid is...

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: trying to get everybody to be experts in everything.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We don't actually need that.

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: We need people to be good at the things that they do and then figure out how to refer and cross-refer and build together, which, again, as Commissioner mentioned, is really the model of the FJCs, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: It's like we have legal staff that do legal services and mental health staff do mental health services, and they don't try and do the same thing, right?

utterances.speaker: Saloni Sethi
utterances.text: And that's kind of what we want to try and build on is that true collaboration where people hold their own piece and understand and respect sort of how they connect to the other work.

chapters.summary: Farías asks how OCS and NGBV will address domestic violence alongside poverty and homelessness. Delany-Brumsey says the work involves social determinants and drivers of violence, flexible funding, emergency housing, and long-term infrastructure.
chapters.title: Farías asks how OCS will address poverty and homelessness intersections

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I think a lot of the questions that have been risen for me during this process is like, how are we talking about this work

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: that involves poverty and those structures that we have throughout our city, even the intersection of domestic violence and homelessness across New York?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How are...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How will OCS address some of those issues in collaboration with or, you know, through NGBV?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just wanting to make sure that we understand what the leading causes are.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We understand we're trying to create a comprehensive approach, but how are we going to ensure that that is actually happening, you know, under this larger umbrella?

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That is the work, figuring out how do we ensure that we're building an infrastructure that prevents harm, that responds to people in

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: the aftermath of really terrible harm, that supports them in the long term.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: That not only means focusing on the individual, it means focusing on the...

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: as they live, the social structures that they're embedded in, finding ways to ensure that we are addressing those kind of underlying drivers or the social determinants of health, the way I think about it.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: drivers of violence.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And that's a core principle of how I approach this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: I think what's been nice is that feels like a very core principle for how the commissioner approaches this work.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: And so I can't tell you the exact how other than we do have some programs that acknowledge this, you know, that focus on providing flexible funding to people, focus on getting them emergency housing.

utterances.speaker: Ayesha Delany-Brumsey
utterances.text: But that is the absolute work of this office.

chapters.title: Farías ends agency Q&A and excuses panel

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I don't have any other additional questions.

utterances.text: Okay, with that, this panel is now excused.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías

chapters.summary: Deputy Executive Director of VIP, a Latine survivor-led organization, describes 5,000 helpline calls and 3,500 survivors served annually. She supports placing NGBV with OCS but demands survivor voices shape strategy and that NGBV receive resources and leadership role.
chapters.title: Rosana Conforme Campuzano testifies for Violence Intervention Program

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Chairperson Farias and the members of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: My name is Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Rosana Conforme Campuzano, and I'm the Deputy Executive Director of Programs at the Violence Intervention Program, also known as VIP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: VIP is a member of the NGBV Advisory Council and is the only organization in New York City led by and for Latine survivors of domestic and sexual violence with a mission to end abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Every year we field over 5,000 calls to our helpline and our culturally specific programs serve over 3,500 survivors and children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: We mainly serve single immigrant mothers of color, many living on less than $15,000 a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Many survivors in our communities face economic and cultural barriers and distrust law enforcement, making it harder for them to report gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: That's why VIP launched a restorative justice program to offer a different path for survivors, a path rooted in community accountability, healing, and repair beyond the carceral system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: For this reason, we were thrilled to hear Mayor Mandani's announcement of the Office of Community Safety because his vision reflects what survivors and community organizations long called for,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: which is a shift away from over-reliance on law enforcement as a primary response to interpersonal and community violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: We deeply believe that placing NGVV with OCS can lead to innovative community-led strategies and elevate survivor leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: But survivors and organizations they trust must help shape the work from the start.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Community safety cannot be built for survivors without survivors at the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: So we are city council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: administration to include survivor voices in organizations like VAP and OCS strategy planning and to give NGBV the resources supporting leadership role needed so that OCS can achieve its ambitious goal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: As Domestic Violence Awareness Month begins tomorrow, we invite Mary Mandani, Deputy Mayor Francois, and the leadership at OCS to spotlight this issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: We ask the mayor to use his significant media presence to showcase the administration's stance against gender-based violence and to uplift NGBV as a mission-critical part of OCS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: VIP is excited, ready, and willing to partner with the administration and city council to create the answers that survivors need and deserve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

chapters.summary: Kluger says gender-based violence is a distinct crisis affecting housing, homelessness, poverty, child care, health, immigration, and economic security. She criticizes the EO15 restructuring as diminishing NGBV and lacking survivor consultation, and urges restoring a standalone office.

utterances.text: My name is Judy Harris-Kluger, and I am the CEO of Sanctuary for Families, New York's largest provider of comprehensive services dedicated exclusively to survivors of domestic violence, human trafficking, and related forms of gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Farias and the Committee on Women and Equity, for convening this hearing and the opportunity to testify here.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Gender-based violence is not a secondary issue that can be absorbed in a broader public safety portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: It is a complex and distinct crisis that touches nearly every part of city government, including housing, homelessness, poverty, child care, public health, criminal justice, immigration, and economic security.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: More than one in five families in the shelter system identified domestic violence as the reason that they entered shelter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Addressing a crisis of this scope requires a dedicated office with the authority, expertise, visibility, and accountability to coordinate the city's response across agencies and to ensure that survivors remain a clear priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: For that reason, we are deeply concerned by the decision to place NGBV within the Office of Community Safety with a diminishing status.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Survivor advocates were only belatedly included in the mayor's transition committee and not at all in the subsequent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: planning discussion around this change.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: And the abrupt announcement under EO-15 in March came as a surprise to the field, subsuming NGBV within a larger office risk diluting its mission and obscuring responsibility of who in the administration is addressing the need of survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: A standalone office gives gender-based violence a visible place in city government and creates a clear point of leadership for services, survivors, service providers, agency, and the public.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: It can set a citywide strategy, coordinate directly with agencies whose policies affect survivors, identify gaps in services, and elevate.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Urgent funding needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Addressing gender-based violence through a trauma-informed, culturally responsive policy shaped by survivors and experienced advocates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: These issues intersect directly with public safety, but they cannot be addressed solely through a general public safety framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Moving forward, we stand ready to work with Deputy Mayor Francois and Community Safety Commissioner DeLayde Brumsey.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: We appreciate the commitment that the Deputy Mayor will join quarterly advisory council meetings to hear from advocates and track progress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Tomorrow, October 1st.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Marks the beginning of Domestic Violence Awareness Month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: And I share with my colleague on the right that this is an opportunity for the mayor to affirm that ending gender-based violence is a core city priority.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: welcome the administration's recent investments and commitments, but programs and funding require a durable governmental structure to coordinate implementation, measure progress, and ensure accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: We therefore urge the administration to restore and maintain a standalone office with sufficient resources, authority, and direct access to senior leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Preserve NGB's specialized expertise, and establish sustained partnership with survivors and advocates.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: The city's structure should reflect the scale and urgency of this crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Thank you for your time and for beginning this important discussion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: We look forward to working with the council and the administration to ensure that New York City maintains dedicated, accountable leadership in gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If we can just take a pause for one minute, Sergeant, can you?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Come hither, so I have a question.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So just for folks that are going to be testifying, the clock is working, but the sound for the buzzer is not.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So the sergeant is going to announce when time is expired.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And the buzzer is not that effective anyway, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Safe Horizon CEO says OCS leaders are thoughtful but criticizes downgrading NGBV leadership, adding layers, and potential title and salary changes that could harm expertise. She warns the CVAP RFP reduces funding while adding requirements and will lower precinct-based reach.
chapters.title: Liz Roberts testifies for Safe Horizon on concerns with restructuring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Farias, Speaker Manon, members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: My name is Liz Roberts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: I'm the CEO of Safe Horizon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We're the nation's largest nonprofit victim assistance organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We're very grateful that the council is examining this issue so carefully.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We will say, having met with both Deputy Mayor Francois and Commissioner Delaney Brumsey, we have found them to be thoughtful leaders with a deep commitment to creating safer communities for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We recognize the value of placing NGBV within the Office of Community Safety, but we have many concerns about the way this decision was made and the impact it is having.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We feel strongly that the leadership of NGBV should not

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: have been downgraded from commissioner to director, and that the new organizational chart adds additional and unnecessary layers between the leadership of this critical office and Deputy Mayor Francois.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: I also have serious concerns having listened to the testimony of the administration a few minutes ago

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: with what will happen to the staffing, the current staffing of experts at NGBV when their titles change and when their salaries potentially change, as was indicated was possible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: I think it will be hard to recruit people with that level of expertise and experience at the lower titles that are envisioned for the office in the future.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: And so while the work of NGBV has continued uninterrupted, that may not be the case going forward because of the plan to downgrade titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: I think, you know, our biggest concern has been that this new structure sends a message that addressing domestic violence, sexual assault, human trafficking, other forms of gender-based violence simply isn't a priority for this administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: And the mayor's silence has only added to that message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: So I would be remiss if I fail for seconds very quickly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: The Crime Victim Assistance Program, RFP, issued at the beginning of September, actually is asking the organization that staffs the precincts to do more work with less funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: It will have a very serious impact on the level of staffing, coverage, and responsiveness that the CVAP program can provide to people who have reached out to the police for assistance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We were reaching 50,000 people before the Adams administration's peg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: That went down to 40,000 because of the peg.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: It will go down even more because of this RFP.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: It adds new requirements while reducing the funding for the precinct-based advocate in a very significant way.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: And we think that we've asked the administration to reconsider, and we think that the council should look more closely at that issue as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Womankind Chief Program Officer says the organization serves nearly 3,000 survivors annually in 18 languages. She urges that success be measured by impact on the most affected and that culturally specific organizations be engaged as partners from the beginning.
chapters.title: Alina Victor testifies for Womankind on culturally specific services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Hi, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: My name is Alina Victor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: So, sorry, good morning, Chair and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: My name is Alina Victor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: I am the Chief Program Officer at Womankind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify on restructuring the Mayor's Office to end domestic and gender-based violence under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: For more than 44 years, Womankind has supported survivors of gender-based violence, particularly immigrant survivors who are often excluded from mainstream services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We serve nearly 3,000 survivors annually in 18 languages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: As the committee evaluates this restructuring, we urge you to begin with a simple standard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Success should be measured by its impact on the most affected by violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We recognize the opportunities this transition presents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Survivors do not experience violence in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Survivors'experiences aren't inherently intersectional.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Many navigating poverty, housing instability, mental health challenges, discrimination, immigration-related barriers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: and language access challenges, while also holding multiple identities that shape how they experience violence, access support, and move forward towards safety and healing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: A more coordinated approach to safety, healing, and stability that truly sees and hears a survivor's experience is important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Culturally specific organizations must remain central to this work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Led by and accountable to the communities they serve, they center the people historically excluded from mainstream.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: and build on cultural traditions, lived experiences, and community strengths to help survivors heal and thrive.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Organizations like Womankind bring trusted relationships built over decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We serve as bridges between communities and systems, elevating the voices of survivors whose experiences are often absent from policy conversations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We exist to serve survivors, confront violence at its root, and build a future free from violence in a way that honors, strengthens, and uplifts cultures and the communities we call home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: As New York City develops a broader vision for community safety, culturally specific organizations should not be consulted at the end of the process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We should be engaged as meaningful partners from beginning to help shape policies and solutions to reflect the realities of the most impacted communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rico describes New Destiny's housing work and NGBV Advisory Council membership, asking that gender-based violence retain dedicated senior leadership and that Family Justice Centers remain a front door. She also warns that NYCHA emergency housing vouchers funding runs out in November and some 2,000 households remain unmatched.
chapters.title: Maritza Rico testifies for New Destiny Housing on preserving FJCs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Farias and members of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: My name is Maritza Rico, and I am the Policy and Advocacy Manager at New Destiny Housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: New Destiny provides permanent housing for survivors of domestic violence to break the cycle of abuse and homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We develop and operate supportive housing for survivors and their families, and we provide housing navigation and aftercare, helping survivors find an apartment and the services that keep them stable in it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We are also a proud member of NGVV's Advisory Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: I want to begin with what NGVB has meant for our work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Our staff are co-located in family justice centers in all five boroughs, which are overseen by NGVB.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: There, we connect survivors to housing resources every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: The daily working relationship has made countless connections to housing possible for New Yorkers who had nowhere else to turn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: NGVB leadership has also been an invaluable partner in fighting for housing subsidies, flexible funds, and other resources survivors tell them they need the most.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We understand the goal of a more coordinated approach to community safety, and we want this restructuring to succeed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Earlier this year, New Destiny joined our fellow advisory council members in writing to the mayor with our concerns, and we appreciate the administration's response,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: including Deputy Mayor Francois'commitment to attend our quarterly meetings and the recognition that NGVB and its network of partners are a model for the Office of Community Safety overall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We ask that this commitment extend to the design of the transition.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: itself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Two things matter most to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: One, that gender-based violence work retains dedicated senior leadership with real standing at City Hall, someone whose top priority is the tens of thousands of New Yorkers who become

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: homeless each year because of abuse, and the thousands more who need services to survive and heal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And two, that the Family Justice Centers and NGBB's role as a front door for survivors are preserved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: New York City has the best-in-class model with impressive quality, coordination, and breadth of trauma-informed services available to survivors and their families.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: The administration's letter...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: May I please wrap?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: I have one more paragraph.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: The administration's letter rightly acknowledged that more work remains at the intersection of gender-based violence and housing, and I want to close on an example of why we need this attention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And I thank you and your staff, Dan in particular, for meeting with us about this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: NYCHA administers close to 4,800 emergency housing vouchers, including more than 1,000 survivor-led households, and the funding runs out in November.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: City Hall and NYCHA have done an extraordinary job with limited resources to find options for households losing this federally funded voucher.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: But about 2,000 households have not yet been matched to any alternatives, and time is running out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We have been urging the city to use CityFEP as a solution of last resort, and that moment has arrived because survivors reach safety without passing through DHS shelter, some from HRA domestic violence shelters, others directly from fleeing their home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: and they are not eligible for city FEPS.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Inexplicably, eligibility requires a DHS shelter history that an HRA shelter stay does not satisfy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: DSS can fix this administratively by designating NYCHA EHV households as qualifying referrals under the existing category for preventing shelter entry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: We would welcome the chance to work through the details with DSS and with this committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you again for the opportunity to testify.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what areas the city is not considering in preventing gender-based violence. Liz Roberts says the city lacks a comprehensive primary prevention plan across all ages and communities.
chapters.title: Farías asks first panel what city is not considering in prevention

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you folks so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I just have two questions for anyone that would like to answer.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What are some of the areas the city is not considering when it comes to preventing gender-based violence?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That's my first question for anyone.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: I think there should be a comprehensive prevention plan that's much more expansive and ambitious than what we have in place now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: We should be doing primary prevention of gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Liz Roberts
utterances.text: At all ages and in all communities, and we simply haven't invested as a city in that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Any other thoughts?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Victor says culturally specific services are often reduced to language access, but immigrant survivors face broader barriers including immigration-related stress and family dynamics that need closer attention.
chapters.title: Alina Victor says cultural specificity is more than language access

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: I would like to add, and I'm going to maybe be,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: like repetitive in this, but I think a lot of the times when we're thinking about gender-based violence, we leave culturally specific and silo it into language access.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: And that is not the only aspect of services that are needed for immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: We're living in a time where immigration services are extremely difficult for a lot of our survivors and accessing that support, though I know there's limitations because the federal government is involved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: It creates other violence opportunities and concerns and contributors within our family dynamics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Alina Victor
utterances.text: And those are things that we also have to look at a little bit more closely.

chapters.summary: Rico says the administration acknowledges the housing and domestic violence intersection but the city must address domestic violence as a top cause of homelessness; NGBV has been a bridge to housing agencies.
chapters.title: Maritza Rico highlights housing as top DV-related need

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And if I may, one last thing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: As I said already, the administration acknowledged that the intersection between housing and domestic violence needs to be addressed a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And we're always pushing for that, as we all here understand that the top reason for homelessness in New York City is domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And NGBB has done an incredible job at sort of being our bridge to some of the housing agencies in the city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: And we hope that that continues to happen.

chapters.summary: Campuzano says gender justice has been absent from the administration's messaging, especially affordability. She notes domestic violence drives homelessness and gender inequity fuels cyclical poverty and financial entrapment.
chapters.title: Rosana Conforme Campuzano says gender justice is economic justice

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: And I just want to add as well, one thing I wasn't able to add in the first time because I was trying to stay within two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: So in truth, we were deeply concerned that gender justice has not been part of the administration's messaging, especially when it comes to the mayor's affordability agenda.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: We all know that domestic violence is the greatest driver of homelessness in New York City, that gender inequity is a...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: key part of cyclical poverty and the survivors often feel trapped in abusive relationships because they lack financial resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: And so I just want to remind everyone that gender justice is economic justice and New Yorkers deserve policies that recognize this.

chapters.summary: Kluger says survivors need to hear the administration say gender-based violence is important, and they have not heard that since January.
chapters.title: Judy Kluger says survivors need public message from administration

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: I would just add one more thing on survivors need to hear from the administration that this is an important issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: And we haven't heard that since January.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I will elevate all of the messages given to me today.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what successful programs need expansion. Judy Kluger cites youth and Camp Hope, Maritza Rico cites housing navigation and aftercare, Rosana Campuzano cites restorative justice circles, Liz Roberts returns to CVAP, and Alina Victor later describes Pathways to Healing embodiment work.
chapters.title: Farías asks panel for successful programs to expand

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If there are programs that you've seen really great success at in your organization, can you share what those are and what it would take to expand it and or advance that said program?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll discuss our work with young boys and teens, that when Liz talks about prevention,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: the need to send the message when kids are young and that resolving issues should not be with the use of force or control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: And we have a program for young boys and adolescents, as well as a camp that we send kids to that is not funded by any government funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: Five days in upstate New York, it's called Camp Hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Judy Harris Kluger
utterances.text: It's a national model, and it brings young people together to address their trauma, but also build resilience and hope.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: Be quick.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: New Destiny ran an aftercare program alongside our housing navigation services for emergency housing vouchers, and this was privately funded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: But we found through this that survivors need a lot more support than is given right now by the city when they are given a housing voucher because it's so much to juggle,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: you know, the housing search, moving cost, child care, everything that comes along with housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: So we are big supporters of housing navigation, especially, you know, we specialize in domestic violence survivors, but for everyone, but especially for DV survivors, whether that be like through the match pilot program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Maritza Rico
utterances.text: So we are big advocates of making that permanent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: And in VIP, one of the things I had mentioned in my testimony was about our restorative justice program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: We developed that program because many of our survivors I had mentioned before are afraid to go to the police, and they don't really have a lot of trust in the authorities, basically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: So one of the things that we started to do was to survey clients and our survivors specifically on what would be an optional sort of an alternative path.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: And so we talked a lot about restorative justice and what that would look like in terms of community circles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: And many of our survivors were in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: They really wanted to be able to come to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: some kind of resolution when it came to a person who was causing harm, and even just resolutions within their own family, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: Because that's not just happening with the person who's causing harm as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano
utterances.text: So we've been very successful in the past two years being able to do circles and be able to really hone down and help the survivor heal in a different way without necessarily having them become part of a system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosana Conforme Campuzano

chapters.summary: Woodbine says restructuring demotes 25 years of health and human services work without survivor input. She fears lost direct access to leadership, notes federal EHV cuts for survivors, and calls for survivor inclusion, direct cash, timely contracts, and public education.
chapters.title: Stephanie Woodbine testifies as NGBV Advisory Council co-chair

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Good morning Chair Faraias and members of the City Council Gender Equity Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to address the Council regarding the restructure of the Mayor's Office to end gender-based violence under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: My name is Stephanie Woodbine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: I co-chair the Advisory Council at NGBV, and I'm a member of NYU Langone Housing and Health Lab, Speakers Bureau, and PAIR Network Cohort 2.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Serving as a resource for researchers, healthcare providers, and policymakers to better understand topics such as how people lose their housing,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: diverse experiences with homelessness, and ways to improve systems of care for people facing housing challenges.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: The Mayor's Office to End Gender-Based Violence is a base where survivors receive inclusive services and support, not incident-based, by rebuilding their lives after fleeing abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: With a swipe of a pen, 25 years of meaningful health and human services work was reduced, and a press conference was held.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: conference called to announce its demotion as a standalone mayoral office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: There was no input from survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: It is perceived as a blow to our safety and how we access culturally competent resources in trauma-informed settings.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: A move to restructure NGBV comes at a time when survivors across the United States continue to receive alarming directives from the federal government, and especially on

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: easy federal cut is to the EHV program created to alleviate the surge in homelessness post-COVID.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Many, many survivors receive these vouchers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: They will be losing their homes and very soon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Surely there will be some carve out for them in the form of a city FEP's full expansion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: But there's also a gap in traditional poverty measures and the actual cost of living in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Robust investments must be made to proven paths of safety for survivors, such as direct cash and timely payments of contracts that is imperative to the viability of said paths.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Harmful social norms perpetrate gender-based and intimate partner violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Survivorship is nuanced and society plays a huge role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Through education and awareness, pervaded narratives about survivors will change if the city leads the charge.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: We have yet to hear from our administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Addressing the issue of domestic violence despite it being a driver of much of the city's most urgent social issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: And we do fear the demotion of NGBV will cut survivors and partner organizations direct access to leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Invite survivors to the policymaking table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Have us as collaborators on next steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: The intention should be transparent partnership and not the diversion of specialized resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: resources for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Finally, gun violence and hate crimes are highest within the survivor community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Reducing gun violence and increasing safety begins with safety in the home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And just a reminder, you're okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yes, a reminder for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: But also, if you want to submit

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: that testimony, any of the additional testimony that's extended, we receive it, we read it to testimony at councils.myc.gov.

utterances.text: You have 72 hours after the hearing.

utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Ghad says Girls for Gender Equity fears the restructuring will deprioritize gender-based violence and survivors. She recommends survivor-centered policymaking, timely contract payments, increased funding for youth survivors, and the mayor speaking publicly against gender-based violence.
chapters.title: Iman Ghad testifies for Girls for Gender Equity

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Good morning, fellow advocates, Chair Farias, and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: My name is Iman Gad, and I'm the manager of policy and advocacy at Girls for Gender Equity, an organization that works intergenerationally through a Black feminist lens to center the leadership of Black girls

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: and gender expansive young people of color.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: As part of our efforts to bring the voices of youth to the forefront of the city, GGE played a vital role in launching the Commission on Gender Equity and has members serving on the Street Harassment Prevention Advisory Board and the NGBV Advisory Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: I'm testifying today on behalf of our organization, our Sisters in Strength youth survivors, and in alignment with the NGBV Advisory Council, where our CEO serves as a member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: While there is no denial that addressing GBV is a vital part of community safety, we still hold the fear that the recent restructuring of the mayor's office to NGBV under OCS will deprioritize GBV and ultimately survivors'needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: We hold this belief because although we have had positive meetings and correspondence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: From this administration as a collective, we simply are not hearing enough public discourse and surrounding the administration's positions and plans to eradicate GBV across the city since assuming office.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: In order to combat the deprioritization of survivors'needs, we pose five recommendations, of which I will read three due to time constraints.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: First, the Office to End GBV should commit to survivor-centered and survivor-led policymaking and programming and follow this commitment by recruiting and consulting survivors, including youth survivors, to work on these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: This framework is essential as the city has not made any significant progress towards reducing the prevalence of intimate partner violence since the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: The city must make timely contract payments to maintain program viability and the survivor safety network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: We also need increased funding to properly respond to more youth survivors and sustain that growth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Third, the mayor should speak out publicly against GBV and create public discourse surrounding the issue, especially as it pertains to community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: These recommendations stem from a recent short survey of our fellow ending GBV colleagues following two specific communications with the administration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Was that the two?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: We shared these recommendations to inform a New York City community safety plan, and they responded with their commitments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Our original recommendations to the administration, however, came from a more comprehensive December 2025 survey, which included addressing survivors'unmet needs for permanent housing, cash assistance, and access to affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: immigration-related legal support, child care, and services for the person causing harm, as well as culturally specific services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: We hope this council and mayoral administration will consider these suggestions as we envision the future of the office to NGPV and see GGE as a resource throughout this transition, especially when it comes to centering the perspectives of youth survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rosado describes survivors navigating disconnected systems and asks who is in charge and what resources remain protected after restructuring. She proposes a 12-month survivor-led domestic violence community hub pilot and says domestic violence is community safety.
chapters.title: Angelina Rosado testifies as survivor and Sisters in Purple co-founder

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm sorry, y'all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Good morning, members of our committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: My name is Angelina Rosado.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I am not only speaking to you as the co-founder and executive director of Sisters in Purple, but I am speaking to you as a survivor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: A survivor who knows what it feels like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: to need safety while being forced to navigate disconnected systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I know where the systems break because I lived it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Domestic violence cannot go reorganized without public view.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Stripped of specialized leadership and treated as one issue amongst many without clear authority, staffing, funding, and accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Response for survivor safety, survivors deserve more than just silence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We deserve to know who's in charge, what resources remain protected, and how is this change going to make us feel safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
