utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So that means it's including police precincts, family and criminal court, ACS, HRA, emergency shelters, mental health care, employment, education, and long-time healing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We see survivors getting handed a list instead of a warm connection.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We see agency fail to communicate eligibility rules that don't match the danger and trusted community organization excluded when the referrals are made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Fragmentation is not a minor inconvenience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: It is for it is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: For survivors in danger.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We understand that the promise of a whole of a government approach, domestic violence is connected to housing instability, poverty, child safety, welfare, mental health, gun violence, and community violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Coordinating this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Coordinating this can save lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm so nervous, y'all.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just asking for it to not buzz while you were testifying.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: You can finish.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, y'all.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Don't be nervous.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This is a safe space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: But coordination without specialized power can create indivisibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: If NGB remains under the Office of Community Safety, it must be recognized, fully staffed, and equipped with funding.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And make sure the leaders are experts, continue to work with direct decision makers, and empower the agencies as a whole.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: New York City, I'm just going to speak from the heart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm not even going to lie.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: New York City must really create a system where we're not just responding to domestic violence, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Like we're actually making a pathway for prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Sisters in Purple does propose a 12-month domestic violence management system pilot that is built around survivor-led community hubs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: This way, it is more than just not having police interaction because we do understand the survivors always do not want to walk into precincts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And they also don't always want to go to where the services are because they are connected to where family courts are, other court systems that can put fear amongst them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: while they're trying to receive services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We ask that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We're not asking the city to pick between domestic violence and community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Domestic violence is community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And a restructure should not be judged by the new organizational charts or new titles, but it should be judged by whether survivors are safe.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Help is easy to reach.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And agencies are accountable and fewer families experience devastating losses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I don't want us to wait for another homicide to happen, another public tragedy to happen, or another oversight hearing for government to act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: You have the authority right now to demand transparency, protect specialized survivor leadership.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And invest in prevention now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I have this for you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: You can begin.

chapters.summary: Martinez recounts being kidnapped with her daughter in 2012 and says the system must do more than respond after harm. She asks whether survivors receive services, whether community organizations are meaningfully included, and whether success is measured by survivor experience.
chapters.title: Angie Martinez testifies as survivor and Sisters in Purple peer director

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: No, I'm a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Okay, peace and blessings and thank you so much to the committee and Women of Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Hi everyone, my name is Angie Martinez and I am the Director of Peer Engagement at Sisters in Purple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: And I'm also a Voices member and also sitting on the FRC Fatality Committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: And I say this with pride.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: I am a proud survivor of domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Back in 2012, I was kidnapped with my daughter.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: By the grace of God, I am here today to tell my story.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Although I had a great team by my side, I still faced challenges while navigating through the system, which shows how much support survivors like me need.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: I am here today because I know personally what it means to need a system that does more than just respond after someone has been harmed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Survivors need a system that sees us, hears us, protects us, and helps us rebuild our lives again.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: That restructuring of the mayor's office to end domestic and gender-based violence under the Office of Community Safety makes oversight incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Under the Executive Order 15, the Office of Community Safety is responsible for coordinating several offices, including NDGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: While NDGBV continues to have responsibilities related to domestic violence services, policies, agents, and services,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: coordination and improving the city's responses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: With that reconstruction comes an important responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We must make sure that survivors do not get lost in the structure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Oversight just asks the questions that survivors and community organizations are asking every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Are survivors actually receiving services when they really need them?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Are our shelters, housing resources, legal services, financial assistance, and safety planning accessible with responsive response?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Are survivors from every borough and every community being heard?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Are community-based organizations being meanfully included in decisions and sitting at the table?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: And most importantly, are we measuring success by what survivors experience?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Not simply by what government agencies report.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: As a survivor, I understand that asking for help can be one of the hardest moments in a person's life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: I was once there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: I was once that person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: When a survivor reaches out, that may be the moment that they have finally found the courage to say, I need help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We cannot afford for that call to be met with confusion, delays, disconnections in the systems, or even death.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: I believe survivors must have a seat at the table, not just as people being served, but as partners in shaping the systems designed to serve us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: As Sisters in Purple, we are committed to making sure survivors'voices remain part of this conversation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: This is why we're here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We need transparency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We need accountability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We need meaningful community engagement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: We need resources to follow the needs of survivors because reconstruction in office is about more than just changing where an agency starts, sits on organizational charts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: It's about whether a survivor feels safer when they reach out for help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: And then I am here today to let you know that we are those survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Listen to survivors, include survivors, invest in survivors, and hold the systems accountable for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angie Martinez
utterances.text: Thank you all and have a blessed day.

chapters.summary: Schuster says URI provides shelter to 4,000 people nightly, 65 percent of them children, and criticizes the restructuring as announced without consultation. She notes more collaborative engagement since then, supports NGBV coordinating services, and urges investment in prevention and abusive partner intervention.
chapters.title: Lauren Schuster testifies for Urban Resource Institute

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I am Lauren Schuster, the Chief External Affairs Officer at Urban Resource Institute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I just want to thank my fellow panelists for sharing, using your voices to uplift survivors that we all serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Frias, members of the committee and staff for holding this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: URI is the largest provider of domestic violence shelter services in the country.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Every night we provide safe housing, sadly, to 4,000 individuals, 65% of whom are children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: 25 years after its creation, NGBV remains an essential voice for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: That role matters today as much as it did back then.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: While other violent crime has dropped, domestic violence rates remain relatively unchanged, particularly in black and Latinx communities in parts of the Bronx and Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: The decision to move NGBV into the Office of Community Safety and to change its leadership was announced without consultation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: That has really defined our partnership over the past two plus decades.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And for a field that's built on trauma-informed practice with transparency and partnership at its very core, that absence of consultation was felt acutely by the providers in the survivor community that we all serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Decisions of this magnitude should be made in the future with survivors and providers at the center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I will say that since then,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And Deputy Mayor Francois and Commissioner Delaney Brumsey have engaged with us in an incredibly collaborative manner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: They visited URI's Midtown office and just yesterday did a walkthrough of the Bronx FJC.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: URI is the contract holder there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: We're encouraged to hear that they're planning a provider advisory council and that they are engaging in an inclusive strategic planning process.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: We believe that NGBV, regardless of where it falls in the org chart, must continue to play a pivotal role in coordinating the services, the supports that survivors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: access when they are in crisis and in need of help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: That is the role that they have played and must continue to play.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: At the same time, we're grateful for the investments that were made in the budget.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: This most recent budget funding was increased to the FJCs, to youth violence prevention, to immigrant legal services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: These are all critical investments for survivors, the families that rely on them and the communities that they live in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I mean, we're really just looking for increased partnership on these and so many more issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I want to highlight just in closing, I know I went way over and I apologize, prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: We speak so much about domestic violence after a horrible situation happens that's in the headlines.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: There's a story of a family annihilation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: We can and should be investing in prevention because there are ways to stop violence before it starts to identify and interrupt those cycles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: of violence, both with youth intervention and also with people who have caused harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And so that is my soapbox, and I appreciate this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Farías asks for gaps in prevention. Iman Ghad says youth need third spaces, mental health support, immigration support, and sustainable funding because gender-based violence is not a one-time issue.
chapters.title: Farías asks second panel what city misses in GBV prevention

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just a question for the providers on the table, same as I asked in the previous panel.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What are some areas the city's not considering when it comes to preventing gender-based violence?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I know some folks have raised some things, but are there things that are hyper-specific to the work that you're doing?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I would love to hear some of that work.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: I would love to echo the sentiment that was just shared, where prevention really does start with educating our young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And so more programming across the board needs to be done because as youth, they're already disempowered.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Sometimes the gender-based violence they are experiencing is at home and they're not empowered enough to even speak about it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: There is no third spaces for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And so, for example, as Girls for Gender Equity, we do serve as a third space for young people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And that is something that is rare in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: But from there, they have to learn to speak about these experiences and learn about them and understand maybe what even is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Going on to be able to identify it as gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And so through our model of we use restorative justice, healing justice, a social work model, and also

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: more recently have been more invested in contributing to the research that goes into allowing young people to dive into the issues that they are seeing in their lives, be able to explore it themselves, and understand what solutions they can come up with.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Through that, that is a huge part of prevention.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Also, mental health support is a huge ask.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: aspect of being able to provide young people with the resources they need to be able to work through the gender-based violence that they are experiencing in their lives, seeing families experience, their friends experience,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: and immigration supports as well, because that is adding a lot more barriers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And ultimately, this issue needs sustainable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Funding because this isn't a one-time issue and it needs for real structural change we need sustainable funding

chapters.summary: Woodbine says the city must invest in helping children of survivors, especially when they enter the carceral system. She shares her own experience with her son's sentencing, custodial court, economic instability, and ACS surveillance.
chapters.title: Stephanie Woodbine calls for support for children of survivors

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: I just have a comment regarding, from a survivor perspective, something that the city needs to invest in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: It's helping children of survivors, especially when they enter the carceral system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: That's important.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: My son has just been sentenced to 25 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: And I should have gotten just a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: My family should have gotten a little bit more of what we needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: But that is definitely one place where we need coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: And now that there's this whole issue of domestic violence and community safety, it's gun violence related.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Why he's where he's at right now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: I was forced to stay in New York because I was in custodial court for 13 years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: And that impacted my son's development, me being in survival mode, my children were right there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Economic instability, homelessness, you name it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: ACS used as a tool.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Of control and the court with their court-ordered surveillance and coercive control that was legal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: So these are certain conversations that survivors need to have out in the open.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Stephanie Woodbine
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Rosado says the city should shift focus from burdening survivors to serving people who cause harm. She describes Sisters in Purple's Brothers in Purple initiative and training gun violence prevention and reentry staff to identify domestic violence.
chapters.title: Angelina Rosado urges prevention and accountability for people causing harm

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: My follow-up question to the survivors that are providing testimony today was, what are some maybe helpful experiences you've had navigating the system, but also where are the points of contention or points of where we have missteps and we're missing?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I appreciate you uplifting that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If anybody else wants to add as well, they can.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Yeah, I think I want to add to your first question.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We're talking about what is missing and what is not really working in reality is, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Leaning in on to prevention, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Making sure that we're just not always focused on survivors and putting burdens on survivors, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: But shifting that energy to the people that are actually causing the harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Actually getting them the proper support and intervention that they need from a holistic standpoint.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So as Sisters in Purple, we actually have an initiative called Brothers in Purple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And our brothers, you know, that comes from a space with people who have self-identified as people that have caused harm

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: and are choosing, again, self-voluntary, are choosing to seek further support and assistance to no longer have the mentality of what they believed was normal, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Hurt people hurt people, and that's the reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And people that cause harm are people that have had a calm cause to them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So when we talk about preventive measures, right, investing, we work with a lot of our CMS organizations, our gun violence prevention and working within that system is also helping training them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Helping training them as survivor led organizations.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We believe that we have the best training, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We are the survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: They learn domestic violence differently when it comes from a survivor-led organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And that's what we have been proving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We have worked with our CMS and also our reentry programs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We have also worked with them and training their staff on how to identify domestic violence, not just for the community that they're serving, but also the people that they are employing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: You know, just as recently, we just had a survivor of domestic violence who worked at a domestic violence shelter in Staten Island who was murdered pregnant in Queens.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: This happened in June.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And yet it is still quiet and we have not heard anything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And to know that the person that caused the harm who is in question is a person who served as a gun violence preventer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And the fact that staff is not trained properly or do they have the supportive resources for them to deal with whatever they are leaving at the door when they enter that organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: People still go home and people still have their own traumas that they're also dealing with on top of asking them to support and protect our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: They also are their own community and they also need that support there, too.

chapters.summary: Schuster says URI operates abusive partner intervention programs that provide accountability-based trauma-informed programming. She cites an Urban Institute evaluation finding reduced recidivism, arguing such investments increase survivor safety and lower long-term city costs.
chapters.title: Lauren Schuster highlights abusive partner intervention programs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Oh, that was on the whole time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: I just wanted to uplift what you said.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Hurt people hurt people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: You or I and many of the other providers here in this room operate abusive partner intervention programs where we provide accountability-based trauma-informed programming to people who have caused harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: For so long, we have relied on survivors to be responsible for ending their own violence without engaging the harming parties in that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And it is true that people who have caused harm have experienced harm.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Almost 80% in research that we've done of people who have caused harm have experienced some sort of trauma prior to that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: URI's APIP program was recently evaluated by the Urban Institute, and it found that it was a promising practice, and it had significant impact on recidivism rates over a 12-month period

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: after successful program completion.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And so it is a real investing in programs that work with people who cause harm has the potential to increase safety for survivors and reduce recidivism so that the city's costs also go down in the long run.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: And so I cannot agree more with all of the points that you made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Lauren Schuster
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ghad says school disciplinary measures mirror the carceral system and traumatized youth are often pushed out. She argues restorative justice in schools is part of ending gender-based violence.
chapters.title: Iman Ghad calls for restorative justice in schools

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And in that same vein, I'd like to also relate how this pertains again to young people and the education that they receive in schools because the disciplinary measures that they have to deal with within schools do reflect the carceral system and it all starts there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: So when sometimes teachers experience a young person who they write off as troubled, usually,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: He's traumatized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Maybe it's experiencing gender-based violence among a plethora of other issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: Again, mental health is a huge part of it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: And what happens is they are usually pushed out of school, suspended, taken out of class, ultimately just taken out of the safety of school, which should be a place where they can learn to understand themselves, the experiences that they are going through, and know how to navigate them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Iman Ghad
utterances.text: So restorative justice within schools is a huge part also of ending gender-based violence.

chapters.summary: Rosado says Sisters in Purple's Future Purple Nation works with schools and shelters to teach youth about domestic violence and teen dating violence. She says children need real resources so they do not carry anger into gun violence and future harm.
chapters.title: Angelina Rosado describes youth prevention work in schools and shelters

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: If I just may add about youth.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So Sisters in Purple, we have Future Purple Nation, which is our youth programming where we work with the schools.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: We come into schools and a lot of it is teachers themselves, their guidance counselors, you know, parent coordinators reaching out to us to make sure, as well as our youth organizations reaching out to us to not just talk about teen dating violence, which is in the month of February.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: But also, a lot of these kids, like Stephanie said, have experienced domestic violence in their households, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So going to the shelters and working with the young people who experienced domestic violence, but help them understand, I was 15 years old when I entered a domestic violence relationship.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: That I was even in one, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So understanding those signs, because the people that came before me in my generation, they weren't allowed to talk about their domestic violence, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Those stories weren't allowed to be told.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: As we see how old Vawa is, even there's the Protection Act against violence on women, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: My grandmother is in her 70s.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: She had no protection, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So these conversations were not normalized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And when we come in,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: into community, we make sure that our young people are really engaged.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: You'd be really surprised how much they care to actually know the information and really absorb it and really implement that in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: I'm a mother of two children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: My daughter's 14.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: She plays no games when it comes to understanding domestic violence, which also helped her really shape friendships, right, in her life and how she created boundaries with people.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And these are the things that are very pivotal to help prevent domestic violence from escalating, teen dating violence from escalating into domestic violence and understanding that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: Our kids are angry, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: They don't have real resources.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And when we talk about the reduction of gun violence, right, if we are not addressing domestic violence in these children's households, they're going to come outside and they're going to be very angry about things, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: And they don't know how to channel that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Angelina Rosado
utterances.text: So leaving domestic violence out of the conversation is really detrimental to our children and our future.

chapters.summary: Farías appreciates the panel's comments, mentions upcoming consent-awareness bills, and excuses the second public panel.
chapters.title: Farías thanks second panel and excuses them

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I appreciate all the comments shared.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I have, it came to mind in this, in your responses here, I have a couple bills around consent and consent awareness.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd love to, as we approach the new year in February, kind of go into schools and continue the conversation with you folks on how we can talk about that in a real way.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'm seeing no questions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: The panel's excused.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Sisters in Purple co-founder and Voices of Women organizer says Black women survivors fall through the cracks whether domestic violence is addressed through NGBV or OCS. She criticizes the lack of survivor inclusion in the restructuring and asks what OCS will do to protect Black women from violence.
chapters.title: Shamara Kelly testifies on Black women survivors and restructuring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: My name is Shamara Kelly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: I am the co-founder of Sisters in Purple.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: I am here today as a community organizer with Voices of Women organizing project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: The Voices of Women is a survivor-led organization that works on systemic change for survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: I want to speak to something that continues to be missing from the conversation about community safety, the lives of Black women survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Whether domestic violence is addressed through NGBV, the Office of Community Safety, or both, Black women survivors tend to fall through the cracks.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: With regard to the restructuring of NGBV, survivors and survivor-led organizations were not included in any conversation leading up to or during the act of restructuring of NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: So we question what the difference is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: What active actions is the Office of Community Safety going to take to protect Black women from violence?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We are watching black women continue to lose their lives to violence and too often there is no public urgency, visibility, or collective response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Office of Community Safety seems more focused on community violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We cannot build domestic violence systems and community safety strategies that respond to some form of violence while remaining silent when violence happens within our homes, families, and relationships and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Part of my concern

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: is the lack of communication from the office

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: of community safety and NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We do not know what this restructuring means for survivors or how they are addressing longstanding issues with the city's response to domestic violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: There just has not been enough communication about what this new structure actually means for domestic violence survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We are organizing for full survivor involvement and implementing policies and procedures that impact survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We should not have to organize for this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: It should be a given that this will happen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Survivors come to the table with solutions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: We should be compensated for their time and certainly deserve more than a statement or condolences after a tragedy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: And our communities deserve leadership that is willing to speak even when speaking is uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: And as someone who works directly with survivors and communities, I know that silence does not make us safer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Survivors need to feel protected and heard.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Shamara Kelly
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ramos describes being abducted and trafficked as a 16-year-old, ACS and OCFS failures, and decades of trauma and instability. She demands extradition and prosecution, independent oversight with paid survivor seats, cross-border tracking, first-responder CNS training, and housing and economic support.
chapters.title: Mildred Ramos testifies on youth trafficking and systemic failures

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair, members of the Committee on Women and Gender Equity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: My name is Mildred Ramos.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I'm an executive leader in nonprofit operations and human services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Coming forward today as a survivor and independent advocate to address systemic gaps in survivor protection and youth human trafficking oversight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Proof that lived experience must lead policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: In 1987, as a 16-year-old girl, I was abducted in Washington Heights, forced into two separate apartments inside the building,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: physically attacked, beaten, and lost consciousness several times while being subjected to severe sexual violence

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: by an adult Dominican man, an adult Jamaican man, a Colombian boy, and a group of diverse boys forced to participate under their direction.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I was examined at North Central Bronx Hospital and reported the crime to the 46th Precinct.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Despite formal records, New York City ACS and New York State OCFS failed to act.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Case stalling permitted me to be trafficked to Arecibo, Puerto Rico, without legal advocacy, tracking, or state care, housed solely by a minor friend.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Unaddressed catastrophic trauma permanently damaged my central nervous system, causing late-onset fibromyalgia with somatic pain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Rather than protection, I faced decades of institutional law.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Systemic blackballing has left me completely without an income for six years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: During a recent Newark emergency, first responders misidentified my trauma as noncompliance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I was forced into a hospital, an experience that deeply re-traumatized me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: The second time I was forced to go, I do not recall everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I remember walking in, being put on an IV, and later waking up to speak with a doctor on a screen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I was discharged alone to spend Thanksgiving dinner isolated in my home, ultimately resulting in the total loss of my family home and stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: In Puerto Rico,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: One-third of the population lives with fibromyalgia, as reported by El Diario de Puerto Rico, amid severe medical shortages.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: And I deeply worry that the people living there will face even worse conditions than what I have endured.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: These are the untold stories of Puerto Rico.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Where our children are sold into modern-day slavery and our people left without health care, while traffickers accelerate gentrification and politicians are silenced by corruption.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: I demand five immediate actions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Extradition and prosecution.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Locate, extradite, and prosecute my abusers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Closing jurisdictional loopholes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Independent Oversight Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Establish a multi-agency body with permanent paid seats for survivors with lived experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Mandatory cross-border tracking.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Link New York City ACS, New York State.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: OCFS, Newark GCPMP, and Puerto Rico Departamento de la Familia.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: First responder CNS training requires citywide training on central nervous system trauma so somatic pain is met with stabilization, not forced hospitalization or hostility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Housing and economic support.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Eliminate administrative barriers to guarantee housing stability and economic recovery pathways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Without survivors leading oversight, institutions use blackballing and lawfare to protect themselves while perpetrators walk free.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Establish this commission, open doors for housing and recovery, and extradite my abusers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Mildred Ramos
utterances.text: Thank you for allowing me to testify today.

chapters.summary: Garcia-Bigelow, a 33-year advocate, lists recent domestic violence homicides and criticizes the mayor's silence. She says NGBV was built with survivors and providers, warns consolidation risks deprioritizing specialized work, and asks for survivor-led policymaking and a real seat at the table.
chapters.title: Madeline Garcia-Bigelow testifies for Domestic Violence Project

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Chair Farias and members of the committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Thank you so much for holding this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: My name is Madeline Garcia-Bigelow.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: I'm the founder and managing director of the Domestic Violence Project housed at the Urban Justice Center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: I have worked on behalf of survivors for 33 years as a DV prosecutor in the Bronx, a civil attorney, and now as a founder.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: In the eight months of this administration, at least six high-profile domestic violence homicides have taken place in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: LaVey Williams, Angelique Apostle, Erica Caldwell, Yesenia Hall, Maria Ines Granda,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: and Dana Foley.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: And yet, we have not heard the mayor condemn domestic violence clearly and unequivocally, even after each of these homicides.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: New York City has spent more than a quarter century building a dedicated survivor-centered system.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: In 2001, through City Charter, the Mayor's Office to Combat Domestic Violence was created.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: And then in 2018, the mission was expanded and it was renamed NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: But these aren't simply titles.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: They embody and symbolize years of advocacy, of conversation, and education led by survivors and providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: It was built with survivors and providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: And even though it collaborates with...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: really closely with law enforcement in the courts, it is decidedly distinct from that.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Executive Order 15 folded that work into the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Consolidation in and of itself is not a disqualifier, but DV is not interchangeable with gun violence interruption or general mental health response.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Survivors have distinct safety planning needs.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: They have distinct confidentiality protections and a justified wariness of anything that looks like general public safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: During July's quarterly crime stats press conference, Commissioner Tisch noted a 6% reduction in major crimes, but pointed out the felony assaults remained flat, with DV accounting for 42% of those assaults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Since the executive order, providers and survivors have not been included in any real conversation about what comes next.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: So when restructuring happens in silence, survivors cannot tell whether a service still exists, advocates can't make accurate referrals, and decades of expertise risk being deprioritized.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: And the need is growing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Since January, in the eight months of this administration, my team of 23 has opened 2,069 new cases.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Our warm line has answered 1,267 calls, more than all the calls received in 2025.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Over 65% of our clients are immigrants, and most of them are undocumented.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: In the most recent issue of City and State asked about the DSA's strong showing in the June primaries, the mayor said his most important goal is delivering for New Yorkers,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: that he is less interested in narrowing who he works with than in expanding who can sit across the table from.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: So we take him at his word.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Mayor Mandani, invite us to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: We ask this council to use its oversight authority to secure a commitment to a survivor-centered, survivor-led policy-making process with an actual, real seat at the table for the survivors and the providers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Madeline Garcia Bigelow
utterances.text: Again, thank you for holding this hearing.

chapters.summary: Katari describes orders of protection not being enforced, case manager turnover, an emergency housing voucher transition, rent arrears, and eviction risk. She says a referral slip is not a service and asks the committee to protect programs, track real outcomes, and preserve NGBV independence.
chapters.title: Luz Katari testifies as survivor on system failures and housing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: My name is Luz Qatari.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am chairwoman of Boricua Power.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am a 40-year-old Boricua mother, survivor, and advocate from Spanish Harbor.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I come to you today as a mother and a survivor and a leader of families who depend on the very office you are reorganizing and moving.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: You are making the decision about survivors without survivors in the room.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: On paper, you call moving NGBV into the larger office of community safety coordination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: To us, it feels like erasure.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: When you move a program, you don't just move an org chart, you move someone's lifeline.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: And that erasure is already happening.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: All the programs that were put in place to keep survivors and our families alive, flexible grants for rent, housing help, legal advocacy, food, clothing, and supplies for our children, on paper they exist.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: But when you actually need them, they feel non-existent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: They are being slowly removed, defunded, or shuffled into other offices where no one is accountable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: No one is asking what happens to a mother and her children when that lifeline disappears.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: This is what that failure looks like in my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I did everything we were told to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I have photos of the abuse, police reports, real-time voicemails threatening my life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: My lawyer wouldn't present that evidence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: The judge did not ask for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Orders of protection were issued and they were not enforced.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: There were no consequences and now four of my five children live with the person who hurt us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: When I saw emergency housing, I was told I was a low priority because he was no longer in the home on paper.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: When I said I was still being threatened, I was told he seemed like he calmed down now.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I stood in a precinct playing death threats of real time out loud for officers and was told to go home and call if he showed up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: He did show up and nothing was done to him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: When I turned to the Family Justice Center, the revolving door continued.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: For almost a year, I have been assigned and reassigned to multiple case managers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Each one promised help with the basics, food and security, clothing, supplies for my child, and most importantly, housing stability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: My emergency housing voucher is being removed from the Section 8 program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I need to transition to a new voucher to keep a roof over me and my 20-month-old daughter's head.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: For months, I have asked for help applying.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: It took forever for someone to finally sit with me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Then at the last minute, I was told there were steps I personally had to take.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Steps that could have cost me my eligibility and my spot.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Steps no one told me about until it was almost too late.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: At the same time this is happening, Section 8 placed multiple rent abatements on my apartment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Management left that balance as my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am now facing eviction for arrears that are not my fault.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I beg to access the grants for family justice advertisers for exactly this.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I emailed, texted, and called every case manager they ever assigned me and their supervisors, and it was silent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: When someone finally called back, I was told the grants were gone and that I should have reached out for an update.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I have the receipts, the emails, the texts, the call logs, providing I did, and proving everything.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: The system did not answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am counted in those 67,733 visits that Family Justice Center says they get.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: But my daughter and I are one missed grant away from losing our home.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: A referral slip is not a service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: We all know how bad it is out there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: NYPD writes up a quarter million domestic incidents a year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: We lose more than 60 New Yorkers a year to domestic violence, half killed by a partner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: The hotline rings nearly 100,000 times, and on any given day across this state, over 1,000 survivors are turned away because there is no capacity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: But those numbers, which I've included on page, for the record, don't show whether a mother actually got help or how long she waited.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: So I'm asking the committee to do what survivors need you to do.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Protect the programs we depend on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Stop quietly removing them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Track real outcomes, not just visits.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: How long to a lawyer, to therapy, to funds, to stable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Audit what you call a service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Preserve NGB's independent and its own director, budget, and trauma-informed staff who understand coercive control and family court.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: And fund consistent, accountable case management and enforce the court orders you issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am not a case number.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: I am Luz Qatari, a mother.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: The system failed me and my children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Don't let it fail the next family.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Luz Katari
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Farías says the bills under consideration include hotline reporting to obtain breakdowns of calls and follow-up, aiming to make data actionable rather than just another data point.
chapters.title: Farías notes hotline reporting bill before Taina Bien-Aimé testimony

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Sorry, and just before you begin, part of the bills that we're hearing today is exactly for that on the hotline.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We need to know the breakdown of the calls and if there's follow-up or not.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And so the council, at least on our side, we're trying to figure out different ways on getting that data and actually be actionable.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Not just another data point that we reference.

chapters.summary: Bien-Aimé, Executive Director of the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women, opposes downgrading NGBV and its commissioner. She says gender-based violence is a grave human rights violation requiring specialized expertise and dedicated infrastructure, and urges maintaining an independent commission headed by a commissioner.
chapters.title: Taina Bien-Aimé testifies against downgrading NGBV

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair for EAS and members of the City Council for this opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: My name is Taina Bien-Aimé.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: I'm the Executive Director of the Coalition Against Trafficking in Women, one of the oldest international organizations dedicated to prevent and end the trafficking and sexual exploitation of women and girls worldwide.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: We do so through legal advocacy and working with a global survivor leadership network.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: We oppose the downgrading of the NGBV commission and its commissioner, which is couched as a simple integration under the Office of Community Safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: Gender-based violence is not a simple subset of general crime or community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: It is a pervasive and grave human rights violation, often perpetrated by members of the community, which requires highly specialized expertise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: dedicated institutional infrastructure, and targeted investments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: The data in our city reflects the critical need for a standalone and independent NGBV commission and commissioner, whether in cases of intimate partner and domestic violence,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: sex crimes and rape, which are increasing in New York City, and specifically for

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: for our organization, the Trafficking in Human Beings for Sexual Exploitation, an acute crisis in New York City that is being largely unaddressed and whose victims are overwhelmingly women.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: I'd also like to take a few seconds to thank the survivors on this panel and in this room for your courage and your leadership and for sharing with the city your lived experiences that will hopefully help us develop

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: comprehensive policies to prevent and end gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: Just on the few testimonies, the searing testimonies we heard today of the brave survivors, it is clear that New York City cannot afford

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé
utterances.text: NGBV Commission as a specialized entity headed by a commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Taina Bien-Aimé

chapters.summary: Mehra, Executive Director of Sakhi for South Asian Survivors, opposes the restructuring and cites high rates of gender-based violence in South Asian communities. She says NGBV must maintain a strong City Hall position and resources and urges investment in community-based services.
chapters.title: Kavita Mehra testifies for Sakhi against restructuring

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Farias and members of the Women and Gender Equity Committee for this opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: My name is Skavit Amara, and I am the Executive Director of SACI for South Asian Survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: I'm here today to testify in opposition to the proposed restructuring of the Mayor's Office to End Domestic and Gender-Based Violence, or NGBV.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Saki has worked with the South Asian and Indo-Caribbean survivors of gender-based violence in New York City since 1989.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: And through this work, we have become acutely aware that gender-based violence is the defining crisis in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: For survivors, it is not an issue that exists in isolation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: It affects their ability to access safe housing, economic stability, food security, education, health care, and community safety.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: That is why the city's response must be strong, coordinated, and centered on survivors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: The urgency of this public health matter is reflected in the experience of the communities we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Among South Asian American New Yorkers, 85% of women between the ages of 18 to 34 report experiencing sexual assault at least once in their lifetime.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: 48% of South Asian Americans report experiencing gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: 41% have witnessed domestic violence in their homes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: And 25% have experienced...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: child sexual abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Behind each of these numbers is a survivor, a family, and a community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: That is why we are deeply concerned about the restructuring that could diminish NGBV standing and access to decision-making in City Hall.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: At a time when survivors and service providers are calling for stronger coordination and greater investment, we should not be creating additional barriers between survivors and institutions responsible for serving them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: A meaningful gender justice movement must be survivor-led.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Survivors must have direct and meaningful voice in the policies and systems that affect their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: They deserve to be seen, believed, heard, and included in decisions about their communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: A reorganization that buries NGBV deeper in bureaucracy with no constitution sends the opposite message.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Saki welcomed Mayor Mamdani to our Iftar in March, and we appreciated the opportunity to welcome him in our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: But meaningful engagement with survivors and advocates must extend beyond individual moments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: It must be reflected in the structure, authority, and resources of city government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: We look forward to building on this engagement with Commissioner Sethi and working together to strengthen support for this important and often

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: overlooked population.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: For these reasons, Saki urges the City Council to oppose the proposed restructuring of NGBV and to ensure that the office maintains strong and

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: meaningful position in the city, in City Hall, and with the authority and resources necessary to lead coordination citywide in response to gender-based violence.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: We also urge the city to strengthen its investment in community-based organizations and services provided directly to survivors every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: If we are committed to a safer, more equitable New York City, survivors must

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: not only have their voice, they must also have a meaningful place in decisions that shape their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.text: Tara Frias, I think one of the things that I didn't hear through the course of this testimony is that this is...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Ultimately the leading public health issue in our city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: And it needs to be addressed as such, and unfortunately it is not.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: When we put NGBV in this scope of community safety, we are not examining the fact that it is a public health matter that is ultimately preventable and solvable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: What we are seeing, particularly for culturally responsive organizations at this moment in time, is just a really critical need, right?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: Like the federal ecosystem that is impacting immigrant communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: 80% of the survivors that we work with at SAKI identify as Muslim.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: We are seeing a really challenging moment between the result of HR1, the changes in

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
utterances.text: We've seen a 14% increase in survivors served over the course of this year, a 50% increase in our food justice program, a 1,000% increase in our legal justice program when we compare the same numbers from last year to this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Kavita Mehra
